2.text: with his foot: it became a woman, very pretty, with thick braids. He said to her, ‘Enter the

3.text: sleeping-room.’ She entered. Before night-fall the Morning Light and the Evening Light came

4.text: together. They said, ‘Oho! who is this?’ — ‘Here we are.’ — ‘Who are you? What did you

5.text: come for?’ — ‘We came to take away your wife.’ — ‘Instead of my wife take this woman, my

6.text: sister.’ Evening Light said, ‘It is well. This wife at least we shall carry off. Let us enter the

7.text: sleeping-room, let us be married.’ — ‘Do not enter the sleeping-room. Return home, take this

8.text: sister of mine with you. Sleep with her at your own home.’ — ‘Well, we agree!’ The woman

9.text: went out. They grabbed her from both sides, carried her home, Evening Light and Morning Light.

10.text: On the way, Evening Light said, ‘Let me lie down first!’ Morning Light answered ‘No, both

11.text: together!’ They came home. Said Morning Light, ‘Let us cook the food first.’ Evening Light

12.text: answered, ‘Let us lie down first; put the woman to sleep.’ The other answered, ‘Let us lie down

13.text: then!’ They went to sleep. Each one kissed her, each one embraced her, both together.”¹

14.text: A form of group-marriage as described in this tale is really genuine

15.text: polyandry. I should also mention the fact that the relations in group-marriage,

16.text: after two or three years, sometimes become complicated through an exchange

17.text: of wives. Each “companion” takes another’s wife, lives with her for several

18.text: months, and then returns her. Sometimes, however, the exchanged wives

19.text: stay with their new husbands for a longer period, or even permanently.

20.text: At the present time the unions through group-marriage² embrace practi-
20.note: Footnote marker ² keyed tight against ‘marriage’, no space, per §2.10; confirmed at 4×.

21.text: cally all Chukchee families. Not to be connected with such a union, means to

22.text: have no friends and good-wishers, and no protectors in case of need; for the
22.note: Confirmed semicolon after ‘need’ at 4×; the book sets a thin space before it, closed per §2.9.

23.text: members of a marriage-group stand nearer to one another than even relations

24.text: in the male line. As pointed out above, however, these two ties often coincide.

25.text: In some cases five or six persons enter into a group-marriage, and all

26.text: enjoy equal marital rights. In other cases a man may have several compan-

27.text: ions in group-marriage who do not stand in a similar relation to one another.

28.text: All Russian women who live in the tundra, married to Chukchee, must

29.text: of course submit to group-marriage regulations. One of these women, an

30.text: elderly widow, proudly declared to me, “My husband never lent me to ordi-

33.text: “It is a common custom for two men living in different villages to agree to become bond-fellows, or brothers

34.text: by adoption. Having made this arrangement, whenever one of the men goes to the other’s village, he is

35.text: received as the bond brother’s guest, and is given the use of his host’s bed with his wife during his stay.

36.text: When the visit is returned, the same favor is extended to the other: consequently neither family knows who

37.text: is the father of the children. Men who have made this arrangement term each other kin-ĭ-g’un; each terms

39.text: south of the Yukon, the last term is sometimes used between the children of two families, where the man has

40.text: married the discarded wife of another.” Lucien M. Turner (Hudson Bay Eskimo, p. 189) says also, “Exchanges

41.text: of wives are frequent, either party being quite happy to be released for a time.” Franz Boas (Central Eskimo,

42.text: p. 579) says the same about the Central Eskimo: “A strange custom permits a man to lend his wife for a

43.text: whole season, or even longer, and to exchange wives, as a sign of friendship.” Murdoch (Point Barrow Eskimo,

44.text: p. 413) says the same about the Point Barrow Eskimo: “A curious custom, most peculiar to these people, is
44.note: Opening quote confirmed curly “ at 4× (not a guillemet, despite how the low-res composite reads).

45.text: the habit of exchanging their wives temporarily.” This custom has been observed at Fury and Hecla Straits

46.text: (Parry, Second Voyage, p. 528), Cumberland Gulf (Kumlien Contributions, p. 16), and in the region about

47.text: Repulse Bay (Schwatka’s Search, p. 197). The same custom existed among some Indian tribes of North America, —

48.text: as A. G. Morice says, “among the Dénés [Athapascan]; and yet, in spite of their good qualities, the temporary
48.note: Dénés is a proper (ethnonym) name, so its accents are kept per §2.15 (only common English loanwords are stripped).

49.text: exchange of wives was not deemed improper at all. It was considered rather the supreme token of friendship,

50.text: an act of unsurpassed hospitality” (Annual Archæological Report, 1905, Toronto, p. 196).
